candidate.answerReason: The three disjoint possibilities for the unique equal pair contribute 95, 95, and 35 triples, totaling 225.

methods.label: Classify the unique equal pair
methods.explanation:
Exactly two distinct values among three expressions means that one pair is equal and the remaining expression is different. Counting according to that unique equal pair will therefore include every valid triple exactly once.

First classify the relevant powers. The values of \(i^x\) cycle through \(1,i,-1,-i\), each occurring five times for \(0\le x<20\). In particular, \(i^x=1\) for \(x=0,4,8,12,16\). Also,
\[
(1+i)^0=1,\quad (1+i)^1=1+i,\quad (1+i)^2=2i,\quad (1+i)^3=-2+2i,
\]
and \((1+i)^4=-4\). Thus, writing \(y=4k+r\) with \(0\le r<4\), we obtain each power by multiplying the corresponding value above by \((-4)^k\). This shows that \((1+i)^y\) is one of \(1,i,-1,-i\) only when \(y=0\). It is a nonnegative integer only when \(y\) is a multiple of \(8\); in the allowed range, the resulting values are \(1,16,256\). Consequently, the only possibilities for \((1+i)^y=z<20\) are \((y,z)=(0,1)\) and \((8,16)\).

If \(i^x=(1+i)^y\ne z\), then \(y=0\), there are five choices of \(x\), and \(z\) can be any of the 19 allowed integers other than \(1\). This gives \(5\cdot19=95\) triples.

If \(i^x=z\ne(1+i)^y\), then \(z=1\), there are five choices of \(x\), and \(y\) can be any of the 19 values other than \(0\). This gives another \(95\) triples.

If \((1+i)^y=z\ne i^x\), the pair \((y,z)=(0,1)\) allows the 15 values of \(x\) for which \(i^x\ne1\). The pair \((y,z)=(8,16)\) allows all 20 values of \(x\), since no power of \(i\) equals \(16\). This gives \(15+20=35\) triples.

The cases are disjoint and exhaustive, so the answer is
\[
95+95+35=\boxed{225},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
